title: Temple Pillars
speaker: Eko Jeff Kelley
summary: Eko Jeff Kelley takes up the practice of "following the body" and Dogen's Eihei Koroku passage "Jumping and Stumbling in a Fragrant World," in which temple pillars and lanterns expound the Dharma. Eko draws on Suzuki Roshi's reading of Dogen on teachers and sincere practice, then describes offering incense behind a teacher, folding a robe in the dokusan room, and the intimacy of eating oryoki together. Bowing to a teacher becomes a freedom from needing to be equal, better, or less, and the roles of teacher and student can be switched. Eko recalls four wooden pillars in the St. Paul zendo and ends with sixteen people coming to dokusan the day before.

sentences.text: Good morning everyone.
Good morning.
Nice to see you.
This seat here at Red Cedar is beginning more and more to feel like home, in a very nice way.
By my count, this is our fifth joint rohatsu.
I'm counting by all the different places I've stayed while I was here.
I can't remember, oh yeah.
But it's a very sweet thing that we do together, and I always have to acknowledge that during this retreat, Red Cedar does almost all the work.
But we are hosting a retreat, a sesshin, at Camp Indianola in September for the third year this year.
So we're trying to encourage Red Cedar folks to come down and have the favor returned, if you will.
It's a lot of work.
Another reason this seat feels like home is because when we assemble this practice container, we invoke all the Buddhas and ancestors that have gone before us, both men and women.
And in doing this practice, we are following their practice.
And so, in a very real way, we are supported by them.
And the more I practice, the more I feel that.
We follow them not only in succession over time, but our teachers and ancestors, in particular the teachers we practice with, we follow them in a more literal way.
We do this practice called following the body.
We don't talk about it a whole lot in our sangha thus far, but when we do this retreat practice together, it really becomes alive.
Following the body, it's a strange thing.
The student follows the teacher's body.
They bow like the teacher bows and sit like the teacher sits.
I notice Tim and I offer incense in a slightly different way.
My teacher offers it like this, and Norman holds it for a minute and then puts it in.
But by doing what our teacher does in that way, by doing what our ancestors have done, we let go of something of our own and open up to something larger than ourselves.
Tim's story of when he and Norman spent the day together, a quiet day, it seems to me a case of following the body, learning by doing.
Intimacy develops there that is hard to describe, hard to put into words.
Going back to the Suzuki Roshi passage that Tim was quoting yesterday:
*Because we want to find out the actual value of the teaching, we practice then and train ourselves to have the actual living meaning of the scriptures.*
I think that's what sesshin does.
It brings out the actual living meaning.
It's not words.
It's not ideas.
It's doing this together.
And how else to describe it?
Manifesting the actual living meaning of the teachings.
Suzuki Roshi goes on:
*But this practice must be quite serious.
If we're not serious enough, the practice will not work and the teaching will not satisfy you.
If you have a serious friend or teacher, you will believe in Buddhism.
Without an actual living example, it is very difficult to believe or practice.
So to believe in your master and be sincere, that is enlightenment.*
So we say, oneness of enlightenment and sincere practice.
The word master for us is a little bit, we don't really use that.
But nevertheless, the teacher does his or her best to model the practice in a way that is helpful to the student.
And I very much believe that without the living example of my teachers, it wouldn't be practice.
I wouldn't be here today, certainly.
This following the body practice, it's most evident, I think, for the Jisha.
John followed me in here this morning.
And this temple is beginning to do this, I guess would be called a Jindo, going from altar to altar and offering incense at more than one altar at the time.
So in our rural temple in Minnesota, early in the morning, starting in the kitchen with six lit sticks of incense, going to the bathhouse, the toilet rooms, the Founder's Hall.
I think there was another one in the house.
And then finally to the Jindo.
These are outdoors, maybe there's a moon out, maybe it's foggy, teachers walking ahead.
Something happens, an intimacy develops.
Eating oryoki together, intimacy develops.
My partner Ken, we've gotten to know each other quite a bit in a certain way, just by serving each other and passing the pots.
So, a little more about this teacher thing.

For me, relating to someone as a teacher has been a great opening to just say, "I trust you enough to follow you in this way, to offer incense as you offer it, to speak as you speak, to sit as you sit."
Not to canvas all the Soto Zen practice in America and say, "Well, I like to offer incense that way, the way they do in Massachusetts."
It's not that, right?
It's to say, "I'm not going to pick and choose, I'm just going to receive."
And that's setting aside our own preferences, our own resistances.
There's this horizontal set of relationships that can be a little bit like bumper cars, we're all jostling.
But then when we allow someone to sit in the teacher's seat and we take the student's seat, I think that is ventilated, that's opened up.
To bow with humility, it's really, for me, freedom.
It's letting go of needing to be equal, needing to be better, needing to be less.
It's just bowing.
And at the same time, I still love to be in the student's seat.
There are several teachers, including my own, that it's a great experience to go in and bow and sit in dokusan and receive them as the teacher.
If I can keep my student practice alive and my teacher practice alive, then things are fluid and ventilated.
In a way, these are roles that we're playing, right?
We agree to play these roles.
And those of us sitting in the teacher's seat have some training, but it's really, okay, I agree to sit here and you agree to sit there.
And then other times we'll switch around perhaps.
But being able to go in and out of the roles with some fluidity is very helpful.
I started to lead John into the zendo this morning and John said, "You forgot to offer incense."
I said, "Oh yeah."
It goes both ways.
And this is not about handing ourselves over to the teacher, right?
Maybe there's guru practice that is that way, that works some places, but in the West here in the 21st century, certainly in Soto Zen, we don't see it that way.
I do think we are giving ourselves to the universe, let's say, and looking to the teacher as a model of how that might look.
Given their particular circumstances and conditioning, what does it look like to give ourselves away in the way that practice asks us to?
If you try to give yourself to the teacher and say, "Here teacher, I'm putting myself in your hands," hopefully the teacher will say, "No, thank you.
Please take that back and we'll do this together."
I think that's how we, in this tradition, enact these roles.
But opening in this way asks a lot of us.
There's a lot of letting go throughout this practice.
And I think what the practice asks of us is to allow ourselves to be transformed in a way we can't imagine.
It asks us to allow ourselves to be transformed in a way we can't imagine.
It's not to put ourselves in a different shape.
It's not to be who we think we should be.
It's not to be the enlightened person that we have an idea about.
It's to actually allow ourselves to be transformed in a way that, when we're all caught up in ourselves, doesn't even compute.
And again, this is liberating to me because I don't have to try to control.
I don't have to be a certain way.
Just really giving myself over to this transformative process.
And then once some of that transformation happens, you say, "Oh yeah, of course.
I didn't imagine that, but it seems so natural."
And later when we're all caught up, it's just not available.
The reality of it is not available to the imagination.
But that points to the expansiveness of this practice, that we go beyond what we imagine.
We allow ourselves to be transformed beyond what we can imagine.
And that's pretty scary, right?
So most of us do this little by little, gradually stop imagining what it's going to be like and just open to what is.
Going back to Suzuki Roshi.
So Dogen said:
*If you want to listen to a Zen master for absolute truth, you must not think about his rank, his accomplishments, deeds, or shortcomings.
Accept him just as he is because he is a bodhisattva.
That is the right attitude toward life.
Just accept it.*
So again, it's not a matter of finding the person who is absolutely a true bodhisattva.
It's being willing to relate to somebody who's practiced being a bodhisattva for a while and allow that person to be a bodhisattva in your life.
It's practice, right?
Because ultimately we want to meet everyone as bodhisattvas.
Just following the body thing.
Nonin Chowaney, who's abbot of the, I think it's a Prairie Zen Center in Nebraska, said he was in Japan for, I don't know, a year or so.
Teacher never gave a dharma talk and never did dokusan.
It was just following the body.
He was bowing, he was eating.
When I was jisha for my first teacher, Dosho Port, he actually had us follow him into the dokusan room and fold his okesa for him.
I guess that's not that common.
At the time I thought it was pretty sweet.
Later I thought, ooh, that's kind of creepy.
But now I'm back to thinking, oh, that's real intimacy.
So whether we go that route or not, I still appreciate the intimacy of that.
And my other teacher, Judith Regear, she came to Seattle to do six jukais for our sangha before I was transmitted.
Similar to Tim's experience, a couple of days just in our living room, folding papers and she was doing the calligraphy.
To do this practice together like that, that's one of the great things about these crazy forms: we do them together.
We orchestrate and we rub up against each other emotionally and we work it out and intimacy develops.
Again, we're modeling or we're training to be intimate with all of our life.
Everything that arises.
Once more from Suzuki Roshi.
So Dogen said:
*Everyone is your master.
Don't pay any attention to whether they are layman or priest or woman or man, young or old.
Everyone is your teacher and your friend.
But as long as you discriminate this from that, you will not meet [unclear: "his end master"].*
As long as you say, "Well, I think he should be a little different.
I think she should bow a little bit better than that."
*If your attitude is right, everything you hear will be Buddha speaking.
Everything you hear is Buddha speaking.
Then the master is not teacher or student.
The student and the teacher are Buddha.*
When we're deeply practicing, everything we hear is Buddha speaking.
I think that's a major, well, it's a wonderful teaching of Dogen's that the whole world is Buddha speaking, is Buddha expounding the Dharma.
All things come forth and realize the Buddha in us.
So we do these practices to move in that direction.
I'm going to turn now to the Ehe Karoku.
Some of you may not be familiar with it, but it's a thick volume of short talks that Dogen gave more towards the end of his career to his assembled sangha.
They're quite different in tone than the Shobu Genzo.
They're little nuggets and some of them are pretty opaque, but there's wonderful imagery.
It's hard to find your way through this.
How do you ever find anything in here?
There's how many different talks? 800 or whatever.
But one way to do it is there's this great index.
So if you want to know, well, what did he say about the moon?
Well, you look up moon and then you can see how this image plays out in his teaching.
In this case, I remember that Dogen likes to go on about the temple pillars and the lanterns preaching the Dharma.
In our St.
Paul's Endo, we had four huge wooden pieces of tree as pillars.
It was an old warehouse building.
They were a problem because you couldn't see through them, but they really anchored down that space.
So here's Dogen, one of the short nuggets of the Ehe Koroku:
*Taking a step forward or backward at the top of a 100-foot pole, with a single mind turn your face and transform yourself.
This mountain monk, Dogen, will allow the pillars and lanterns to expound this principle for everyone.
Have they finished expounding it yet or not?
They expounded it last night and also the night before.
Tomorrow they will expound it and also the day after.
If they have finished expounding it, has everyone heard it or not?*
The pillars and lanterns expounding the Dharma.
Can we hear it?
Can we allow it to enter?
Then going on to one I want to spend a little more time with.
The translators have given these little titles.
The title of this little piece is "Jumping and Stumbling in a Fragrant World."
That's a nice image for what we're doing here.
Jumping and stumbling in a fragrant world.
*When we exhaust our strength to express it, the pillars help us from the sidelines with half a word.
Training the mind and verifying enlightenment, a wooden ladle energetically adds another mouthful of sustenance for practice.*
The pillars are just there giving us a little help.
The wooden ladle, we have that image in our mind, it's offering us something, another mouthful.
*For a person who can hear and who can practice, emotions are not yet born and forms have not yet appeared.
Everything let go.
Voices babbling on, every bit is naked.
Without awakening, advancing each step we stumble over our feet, making seven mistakes and eight mistakes.*
We have that expression, falling down seven times and getting up eight times.
This is making seven mistakes and then making eight mistakes.
One continuous mistake.
*Without awakening, advancing each step, we stumble over our feet.
Without resting, taking a step backward, we stumble over our exposed legs, arriving at two and arriving at three.*
Which according to the translators is just everyday stuff.
Stumbling over our exposed legs.
How often do we get up from zazen?
We feel exposed, right?
One of our feet's gone to sleep, we're stumbling.
But the pillars are there.
They may be in the form of the person next to you, or they may be the solid wall.
The world is there, the universe is there.
This practice container is there.
*Jumping up and kicking over Mount Sumeru, pick it up and place it within everyone's eyeballs.
Stumbling and overturning the great ocean, pick it up and place it within everyone's nostrils.
Why doesn't everyone awaken and understand?
Need I say more?*
This overturning, I think, is a nice image.
Our conventional world is overturned.
And maybe we can see it in people's eyeballs, see it in people's nostrils, embrace it with our eyeballs and nostrils, let it permeate our whole being.
So the format of these little talks is usually there's a paragraph of Dogen talking, and then there's a pause.
After a pause, Dogen says.
So after a pause, when he says, "Why doesn't everyone awaken and understand?"
Pause.
He says:
*Last night a flower blossomed and the world became fragrant.
This morning a fruit ripened and Bodhi matured.*
So this fragrant world in which we are jumping and stumbling and being supported.
Last night a flower blossomed and the world became fragrant.
It is today like that.
This morning fruit ripened and awakening matured.
The moment before this one, a flower bloomed and the world became fragrant.
In this moment the fruit is ripening and awakening matures.
This world is fragrant.
This activity is awakening, the fruit maturing, if we are there with it.
Tonight, this night, a special night, there's no doubt that the tree will be blooming and the world will be fragrant and awakening will ripen.
But it's here.
When we exhaust our strength, anybody hit that point yet?
The pillars help us from the sidelines with half a word.
The ladle energetically adds another mouthful of sustenance for practice.
So when we open, we receive the Dharma from all things, all beings.
Pillars are there, the wooden ladle just when we need it.
So as we move in to the rest of the sesshin, can we just simply open?

Not imagining what might happen, but simply open, giving ourselves to the universe, allowing ourselves to be held and supported by this venerable group of practitioners, these cushions, these walls, these lanterns, allow them to expound the Dharma, to ripen fruit.
Can we open to this mysterious, transformative energy in the universe that wants us to dance?
Can we feel the pain in our legs and what?
Or get up and sit in a chair.
So in the next moment we're ready to be supported and open to all things expounding the Dharma.

Yesterday, I spent most of my day in the Dokusan room and it was so sweet to have, I think, 16 different people come in and open themselves, allow me to sit in the teacher's seat, and they were willing to sit in the student's seat, and we were able to meet because of this incredible practice, one way in which the flower blooms and the fruit ripens.
So thank you so much for your practice and for your support and for coming together to be here.
